overview: The second meeting covered the functional design of the remote control. After the Project Manager recapped the first meeting, the Industrial Designer presented how a remote works (infrared signal, battery power, a chip that encodes button presses) and raised making it smaller and harder to lose; the User Interface Designer proposed a simple, user-friendly flip-top with common functions outside and complex ones inside; and the Marketing Expert presented usability-lab research on 100 people showing that users find remotes ugly, would pay more for a good-looking one, use few buttons, often lose the remote and worry about repetitive strain injury. The Project Manager announced new requirements: no teletext, a TV-only remote, and the corporate image built into the design. The team settled on one product design, a mid-range trendy and business target market, Video Plus codes instead of date and time programming, a rechargeable remote with a docking station, a beeper to find a lost remote, a flip-top that moves away from the usual brown rectangle, and a user-friendly manual rather than an in-store help service. Repetitive strain injury and the choice between buttons and a touch panel stay open. Before the next meeting the User Interface Designer looks into building the company logo into the shape, and the Marketing Expert looks at instruction manuals.

topics.title: Recap of the first meeting
points: Last meeting settled on a universal control, one handset for TV, video and other equipment.
The product should be accessible to a wide age range and reflect the company's image of putting fashion into electronics.
The look should not betray the limited budget, and should be uncluttered and not daunting.
Ideas discussed: a flip-open design, a smaller remote, and an electronic panel for extra features such as programming.

topics.title: Industrial Designer: working design
points: The Marketing Expert asked to present later to gather more information, so the Industrial Designer went first.
A remote is a device that sends a signal to change the TV's state: power, channel or volume.
The design should take ideas from existing products but still stand out.
Most remotes use infrared, which is cheap, and only need to send a little data; TVs already use infrared, so the remote must conform to it.
Most remotes run on AAA batteries, which make them chunky; he asked whether another power source could shrink the remote, considering power consumption.
Main components: power source, a chip that converts button presses into an infrared signal, and an infrared bulb with a range of about five metres, enough for home viewing.
He showed a rough circuit sketch (power to the infrared bulb, chip and interface) and left the external design to the User Interface Designer.
All the components he proposed are low cost.
Small remotes are easy to lose, so he suggested something to stop it going down the side of the sofa; the Marketing Expert said this also came up in market research.

topics.title: User Interface Designer: interface concept
points: Purpose: simplify interaction with the TV and make it as easy to use as possible, with main features such as volume and channel rather than many complex buttons.
Concept: a flip-top model with frequently used functions on top and complex functions (for example programming favourite channels) inside, so it suits a wide audience.
Possible added features: a shock-proof body and a design that appeals to many people.
People often never use 30 to 40 percent of the buttons on a remote after a year.
At the volume implied by the 50 million profit aim, economies of scale could allow more features at lower cost.
The buttons should not become hard after continuous use; consider soft versus hard buttons.
The Project Manager deferred comments to the end of the meeting.

topics.title: Marketing Expert: market research findings
points: Research in the company usability lab observed 100 people, male and female, aged 15 and up, using remote controls.
Overall, users dislike the look and feel of current remote controls.
75 percent find most remote controls ugly.
80 percent would spend more money on a remote that looks fancy, which surprised the team.
Current remotes do not match how people use them: 75 percent zap (channel-hop) a lot, which has power implications.
50 percent of users only use 10 percent of the buttons, so fewer functions could also cut cost.
50 percent were frustrated by losing the remote in the room.
34 percent said remotes take too much time to learn to use.
Slightly more than a quarter said remotes are bad for repetitive strain injury.
Most people aged 35 and under would like an LCD screen and speech recognition; interest evens out at 35 to 45 and reverses in older groups, with many don't-knows among older people.
The Marketing Expert suggested a lost remote could bleep or flash, and offered to email more detailed tables.

topics.title: New project requirements and finding a lost remote
points: No teletext, because consumers consider it outdated now that there is the internet.
The remote is for the TV only, not a combined control, which limits cost and makes it easier to understand.
The team discussed whether TV-only still covers video; combined TV-video units and Sky Plus boxes that record to a hard drive mean they assume play, stop and programming stay.
The User Interface Designer asked whether research covered combined remotes; it did not, but people mostly use basic channel and video buttons and find programming videos a nightmare.
The Industrial Designer said full speech recognition would be expensive and not very good, and suggested a whistle-activated finder like key chains.
The Project Manager pointed to the fixed budget and suggested a button on the TV that makes the remote beep, which sounds cheaper; the Marketing Expert called it a super idea.
The corporate image must be built into the handset: logo, fashionable and trendy, since people pay more for good looks.

topics.title: Designs for different markets, touch panels and ergonomics
points: The Marketing Expert said what is attractive differs by age and country (a trendy New Yorker versus a retired South African), so the fashionable exterior might change per market while the engineering stays the same.
The User Interface Designer asked whether that means one model or five or six; the Industrial Designer said the inside would be the same with different bodies.

The Project Manager noted new remotes have big rubber buttons and, to be original, suggested a touch panel like touch-screen computers that would wear out less, appealing to young office workers in Japan, while still clearly labelled for older people.
The Industrial Designer raised ergonomics: the Xbox needed a smaller controller for Japan because people there have smaller hands, so button size may vary by country.
The User Interface Designer suggested a touch screen could help with repetitive strain injury.
The Project Manager concluded they design one product and the company adapts it, so the team should not get bogged down in variants.

topics.title: Repetitive strain injury and target market
points: The Marketing Expert doubted that moving a finger on a small screen addresses repetitive strain injury, which is caused by small repeated movements, and suggested postponing it to a future meeting.
The only other way round it would be speech recognition, which is extremely expensive.
The Marketing Expert asked whether to start with a younger age group and broaden later; the User Interface Designer suggested focusing on the biggest market, for example ages 20 to 35.
The Project Manager said the company wants a fashionable, trendy product, so the focus is mid-range business-class people even though older generations are a larger population.
The Marketing Expert wanted to avoid wasting marketing budget by focusing on where purchasing power is.

topics.title: Recording with Video Plus
points: The Project Manager suggested Video Plus: TV guides print a five or six digit code after each programme, and entering it sets the recording without dates, times or channels.
It needs at most one extra button because the number buttons are already there.
The feature has existed for a long time but is poorly advertised; Sky boxes can already record a programme or a whole series with one or two presses.

topics.title: In-store help service versus manual and customer service
points: The Marketing Expert suggested a free help service in the company's high street shops, like mobile phone retailers, to reassure older buyers.
The Industrial Designer said phone retailers help because of contracts and was unsure of the cost; the Project Manager said customers would have to bring in their TV to show the problem.
Instead, instruction manuals and a customer service phone line cover support; the User Interface Designer said nobody would walk to a shop for a remote.

topics.title: Instruction manual and batteries
points: The Project Manager said manuals are often tiny writing over many pages and get left in a drawer, so the manual should be user-friendly.
She suggested a mobile-phone-style battery; the Industrial Designer said these are specially made and come with a charger.
Like a cordless house phone, the remote would sit in a charger when not in use, last a long time, and be smaller.
The locator beeper could be on the docking station.
Rechargeable means no buying batteries and is cheaper in the long run.

topics.title: Shape, casing and company logo
points: The shape should be trendy: not a big box with lots of things, and not so tiny that it causes repetitive strain injury.
Most remotes look identical, long brown rectangles with crammed buttons; the team wants to get away from that.
The Project Manager confirmed a flip-screen.
The User Interface Designer described a curved, banana or boat-shaped design (like an older Nokia phone) moulded to the hand so the thumb bends less.
The Project Manager asked to look into the company logo, for example a C-shaped body that opens like a shell; the User Interface Designer preferred a logo in a corner but agreed to look into it.
The Marketing Expert liked a conch or scallop shell exterior in lightweight plastic opening into the flip-top, and thought holding it between the covers could reduce strain.
The Project Manager suggested interchangeable casings like phone fascias, for example psychedelic for young people and sleek for others.
An attractive remote people keep on the mantelpiece is less likely to be lost down the sofa.
The User Interface Designer suggested producing five or six designs and choosing the most appealing.

topics.title: Summary and next steps
points: The Marketing Expert recapped the requirements: no teletext, TV (and by implication video) only, corporate image in the remote, and Video Plus.
Video Plus replaces separate buttons for date and channel; it is mainly an advertising feature and should be explained in the manual.
Rechargeable batteries are included; buttons are not yet a requirement and will be worked out with the design, possibly with market research.
A beeping alarm for a lost remote was discussed; learning to use it should be simple, with few functions, and it should differ from existing remotes.
The Marketing Expert will look at instruction manuals before the next meeting; further questions can be emailed to the Project Manager.

human_not_covered: The remote will have a seashell-like shape (part of the human decision on Video Plus and shape): the shell shape was only proposed and liked; the User Interface Designer agreed to look into it, which is an action item, not a decision.
The shape will accommodate the LCD display (same human decision): no LCD display was agreed in this meeting; it appears only in the research findings and a passing remark.

Multiple casings will be made available (part of the human decision on the docking station and manual): the Project Manager only suggested interchangeable fascias, and the group had just agreed to design one product.
